Whether leukemia is hereditary is a matter of ongoing scientific debate, with sources presenting conflicting perspectives. Several sources assert that leukemia is generally not hereditary: d1 states it "does not tend to run in families and therefore is not usually hereditary," d3 notes that "the mutations are genetic, but usually not hereditary," d8 explicitly states "LGL leukemia is not inherited," d10 reports that "family history does not appear to play a role in the development of CML," and d11 states childhood leukemia "is not thought to be hereditary." On the other hand, other sources highlight a meaningful hereditary component: d2 notes that "researchers are increasingly finding that leukemia may run in a family due to inherited gene mutations," including germline mutations in GATA2, ETV6, CEBPA, and RUNX1; d4 estimates that "5–10% of leukemia cases are attributed to genetic susceptibility" via inherited mutations; d5 reports that first-degree relatives of CLL patients have an approximately 8.5-fold elevated risk; and d12 states that "hereditary hematologic cancers are very likely underdiagnosed." Institutions such as UCLA Health [d6] recognize "hereditary leukemia and hematologic malignancy syndromes" as a distinct category of inherited cancer risk. Overall, the current evidence suggests that while most leukemia cases arise from acquired (non-inherited) mutations, a subset — particularly certain subtypes — does have a hereditary component, and research in this area continues to evolve [d1, d2, d4, d7].
